title: Managing tusks on male pigs
subtitle: Keeping boar tusks at a safe length for handler and herd.
excerpt: Male pigs grow tusks continuously from maturity. Entire boars and castrated males (hogs) can develop tusks long enough to injure handlers, other pigs, or fencing. Tusk clipping with embryotomy wire or a Gigli saw is straightforward once the pig is restrained, and keeps the animals safe to work around.
sourceNotes: AHDB Pork, Managing Boar Tusks fact sheet (2017). Pig Veterinary Society, On-farm tusk trimming guidance (2021). British Pig Association, Boar Management Notes (2018).

glossaryTerms.definition: A flexible serrated wire used in veterinary practice to cut bone. Works well for removing tusk tips without the vibration of powered tools.
A flexible chain saw used in surgery and livestock management. Cuts tusks smoothly with less heat than an electric disc.

content.text: Tusks are canine teeth that grow continuously in intact male pigs and in some castrated males. By 18 months, an entire boar may have tusks 4 to 6 cm long. At 3 to 4 years they can exceed 10 cm and curve upward, creating a real injury risk. Tusk clipping is not painful if done correctly: the tusk has no nerve in the outer third, and cutting above the gum line through this region removes the danger without touching the pulp.

Tusk clipping in the UK is a routine husbandry procedure that a competent keeper can perform. It does not require a veterinary prescription or veterinary attendance, but you must be able to do it competently. If in doubt, ask your vet to demonstrate the first time.

Safe tusk trimming needs a well-restrained pig. A pig snare looped around the upper jaw and secured to a gate keeps the pig's head still and gives you access to the tusk area. Most pigs protest the snare but settle within 30 seconds. Work quickly and calmly.
Have a helper hold the snare while you work on the tusk. Alternatively, secure the snare to a fixed point at snout height.
If the boar is particularly large or aggressive, ask your vet about mild sedation. Trying to work around a thrashing 200 kg boar is the most common cause of injury in this procedure.

Look at the tusk from the side. The gum line is where the tooth meets the gum. Cut the tusk to leave 2 to 3 cm above the gum line. This removes the curved, sharp tip while staying well clear of the pulp cavity, which runs only through the inner third of the tooth near the root.

attrs.title: Do not cut at the gum line

content.text: Cutting flush to the gum or below it exposes the pulp. This is painful, bleeds, and creates an entry point for infection. Leave 2 to 3 cm of tusk above the gum.

Once cut, inspect the cut surface. It should be white and solid. A pink or hollow centre means you have reached the pulp; apply veterinary antiseptic spray and call the vet.

Most boars need tusk trimming every 12 to 18 months. Faster-growing breeds and older animals may need it annually. Check tusk length as part of the quarterly welfare check. Record the date and estimated tusk length before and after in the holding health diary.

attrs.cue: Boar is not restrainable with a snare alone
attrs.cause: Pain from a previous poor experience, or a naturally reactive temperament
attrs.fix: Ask your vet to sedate the animal. Do not attempt tusk trimming without adequate restraint.

attrs.cue: Cut tusk is discoloured brown or shows pink tissue
attrs.cause: Cut was too close to the pulp or the wire was used too slowly, generating heat
attrs.fix: Apply chlorhexidine spray to the cut surface. Monitor for swelling around the jaw in the following week. Consult the vet if swelling appears.
